extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Kant's Groundwork
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating maxims and practical principles according to Kantian moral theory — distinguishing hypothetical vs categorical imperatives, the role of form vs matter of maxims, autonomy, and the universalizability test. Intended to show which principles count as objective moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperatives vs maxims (categorical vs hypothetical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperatives are characterized by 'shall' and express the objective necessitation of an action; maxims are subjective principles. Imperatives that determine the will only in reference to a desired effect are hypothetical imperatives (precepts of skill); imperatives that determine the will as will, without reference to a desired effect, are categorical and alone are practical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothetical imperatives are conditional and serve as practical precepts (e.g., 'be industrious so you won't want in old age'); categorical imperatives are unconditional laws. To assess whether a rule is a law, check whether it determines the will independently of contingent ends or means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material practical principles are empirical and cannot furnish practical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: All practical principles which presuppose an object (matter) of the faculty of desire as the ground of determination of the will are empirical and can furnish no practical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the maxim depends on an object whose desirability is contingent (pleasure, desire), it cannot be known a priori and thus lacks the objective necessity required for a moral law. Such principles may serve as maxims or counsels but not as universally binding laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material practical principles reduce to self-love / private happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: All material practical principles as such are of one and the same kind and come under the general principle of self-love or private happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the determining ground of the will is the expected pleasure or happiness, the principle belongs to 'sense' and not to pure practical reason. Even refined intellectual pleasures, when they determine will via expected pleasure, remain material and empirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must determine the will as will (independent of means or effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws must be sufficient to determine the will as will, even before asking whether I have power sufficient for a desired effect, or the means necessary to produce it; hence they are categorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine moral law cannot presuppose empirical conditions (power, means, expected outcomes). If obedience to a rule depends on whether you can achieve some effect, it is not a moral law but a conditional precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalizability / form-as-criterion (Fundamental Law of Practical Reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act so that the maxim of thy will can always at the same time hold good as a principle of universal legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test a maxim by asking whether it could be willed as a universal law. Use the 'could it be a law for everyone?' test: if universalizing the maxim leads to a contradiction in conception or to annihilation of the maxim's purpose (see depositexample where universal denial of deposits would eliminate deposits), it fails to be a moral law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims must be judged by form not by matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational being cannot regard his maxims as practical universal laws, unless he conceives them as principles which determine the will, not by their matter, but by their form only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract from the matter (the desired object) of a maxim and attend to its formal universalizability. Only the purely formal capacity of a maxim to serve as universal legislation confers on it the character of a moral law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom and unconditional practical law reciprocally imply each other
rubrics_metrics.description: A will which can have its law in nothing but the mere legislative form of the maxim is a free will; freedom and an unconditional practical law reciprocally imply each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral consciousness of an unconditional law leads to the concept of freedom (independence from empirical causality). Conversely, conceiving a free will requires that its law be independent of empirical conditions. Appeals to empirical irresistible impulses do not negate the possibility of moral obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of the will as basis of morality; heteronomy invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: The autonomy of the will is the sole principle of all moral laws and of all duties which conform to them; heteronomy of the elective will cannot be the basis of any obligation and is opposed to morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autonomy = self-legislation (lawgiving by practical reason). Heteronomy = dependence on objects, inclinations, or external commands; if a maxim is heteronomous (determined by matter/empirical conditions) it cannot ground moral obligation even if the resulting action coincides with the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical precepts of skill (technical rules) are not moral laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions which in mathematics or physics are called practical (technical) point out how a certain effect is to be produced and have nothing to do with the determination of the will; they are theoretical in that sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish technical 'how-to' rules (how to achieve an end) from moral prescriptions. Technical rules may be universally applicable in means but do not determine the will as moral law because they presuppose choice of end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective principles lack objective necessity required for law
rubrics_metrics.description: Since susceptibility to pleasure or pain can be known only empirically and cannot hold in the same degree for all rational beings, a principle based on this subjective condition may serve as a maxim for the subject but not as an objective law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral laws must be recognized a priori and be universally and objectively necessary; variability of feelings and desires among subjects prevents subjective/maxim-based principles from being moral laws.
